meta.about: Findings that cut against the grain of what most people assume. Each is load-bearing — it changes how you read the rest of the stack — and each is either derived from the corpus and the cascade, or cited. Weight 3 renders as a full callout, 2 as a compact one, 1 as an inline flag.

notes.title: Most of the silicon in an AI accelerator is memory, not compute
notes.figureNote: memory silicon to logic silicon, by area
notes.body: A Blackwell-class part is two reticle-limited logic dies — roughly 1,600 mm² of compute. Around it sit eight HBM stacks: sixty-four DRAM dies, each inside an 11 × 11 mm package, for something like 6,000–7,500 mm² of memory. Add a CoWoS interposer spanning more than three reticles and the compute die is a minority of the silicon in the package by a wide margin.
notes.soWhat: It reframes the whole supply question. When people say the industry is short of GPUs they usually mean it is short of HBM and the packaging that attaches it — which is why the binding constraint sits in strata 08 and 09 rather than 10, and why memory makers have as much pricing power as the accelerator designer.

source.what: HBM3E — 8- and 12-high stacks of 24 Gb 1β die in an 11 × 11 mm package

notes.title: Running the chip costs far more than making it
notes.figureNote: energy to serve an answer vs. fab energy embodied in the silicon
notes.body: A leading-edge fab burns on the order of 800 kWh per wafer across a thousand process steps and three months — an enormous number that gets quoted often. But it is spent once, and then amortised across every answer that silicon will ever produce over five or six years. The electricity to serve a single answer works out roughly 500 times larger than its share of the fab.
notes.soWhat: Almost every intuition about AI consuming the earth's minerals is pointed at the wrong end of the chain. The materials are close to free at the margin. The constraint is, and has always been, the power station — which is why stratum 13 keeps showing up as the thing that actually limits the build-out.

notes.title: A 26 × 33 mm rectangle explains modern chip design
notes.figureNote: the largest area lithography can print in one exposure
notes.body: The reticle field is a hard optical limit: no scanner can pattern more than about 858 mm² at once. The H100 is 814 mm² — deliberately parked just underneath it. A single monolithic die at Blackwell's transistor count would need roughly 1,000 mm², so it is built instead as two reticle-limited dies stitched together at 10 TB/s.
notes.soWhat: Chiplets and advanced packaging are not a design fashion; they are what happens when a physical constraint stops moving. It is also why stratum 09 became a bottleneck: once you cannot make the die bigger, the only way up is to attach more dies together.

source.what: Blackwell — 208 bn transistors across two reticle-limited dies

notes.title: The thirsty part is the cooling, not the fab
notes.figureNote: datacentre cooling water vs. fab water, per answer
notes.body: A fab draws something like 4,000 litres of ultra-pure water per wafer, and that figure is the one that reaches local news. It is also spent once. Datacentre cooling water is spent on every single request, and per answer it works out roughly 100 times larger.
notes.soWhat: Water fights over semiconductor plants and water fights over data centres are the same argument aimed at very different magnitudes. The one that scales with usage is the one downstream.

notes.title: The quartz that matters is not the quartz in the chip
notes.figureNote: crucible quartz vs. feedstock quartzite, by mass per wafer
notes.body: Making a wafer consumes roughly 570 g of ordinary quartzite as smelter feedstock — widely available, geologically unremarkable. It also consumes about 15 g of high-purity quartz in the Czochralski crucible, which is a consumable destroyed by every pull. The crucible material is the one that comes from a small district around Spruce Pine, North Carolina.
notes.soWhat: The chokepoint is not where the mass is. Thirty-eight times more rock passes through the smelter than through the crucible, and the crucible is the part nobody can substitute on a useful timescale.

notes.title: Asking a model to think costs two orders of magnitude
notes.figureNote: extended reasoning vs. a direct answer, per token
notes.body: Energy per output token spans from roughly 1 × 10⁻⁴ Wh for a small distilled model to 3 × 10⁻³ Wh and beyond for a frontier model generating a long chain of thought. Nothing else in the entire chain — not the fab, not the wafer, not the grid — varies by anything like that factor.
notes.soWhat: The single largest lever on the environmental cost of AI is not the hardware or the grid. It is the routing decision about which model answers which question, made thousands of times a second inside a serving stack.

notes.title: Every leading-edge logic site on Earth would fit inside one mid-sized city
notes.figureNote: ground enclosed by all nine sites, drawn at true scale
notes.body: Draw a circle round each site in the world currently running or bringing up logic at the 5 nm class and below — Hsinchu, Tainan, Taichung, Kaohsiung, Pyeongtaek, Leixlip, Chandler, north Phoenix, Hillsboro — at the real extent of each park or campus. Added together the nine enclose roughly 170 square kilometres. Milan's administrative area is 182. Four of the nine, and the great majority of the capacity, sit on one island, within four hundred kilometres of each other.
notes.soWhat: Concentration in this industry is usually argued in percentages, which are easy to wave away. Measured as ground it stops being an abstraction: the entire physical substrate of machine intelligence is a handful of industrial parks you could drive between in an afternoon, and no amount of capital shortens the three years it takes to pour another one.

notes.title: The longest waits in this stack were not spent inventing anything
notes.figureNote: thirty-year waits that were actually waiting on the science
notes.body: Twelve capabilities on the Lag chart took thirty years or more to get from working to shipping — and only three of them — EUV lithography, silicon-carbide substrates and the combined-cycle turbine — spent that time with the science unfinished. The other nine worked the whole time. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling waited 43 years because air was cheaper. Mixture of experts waited 30 because there were not yet enough parameters for routing between them to pay. Backpropagation waited 42 for something to run on. Atomic layer deposition waited 33 because nothing needed a two-nanometre film.
notes.soWhat: The binding constraint in this industry is rarely an unsolved problem. It is far more often a solved one with no reason to exist yet — which reframes what a technology roadmap is for. If the pattern holds, the capability that unlocks 2040 is already sitting in a journal, and what it is waiting for is not a discovery but a price, a volume or a customer.
